note: Uturunku is the jaguar (Panthera onca), source of Peruvian Spanish 'otorongo'. NOT 'puma', which is the cougar (Puma concolor) and would be a different animal; do not substitute. Jaguars are lowland (Amazonian) animals, so highland children may know the word mainly from stories; the uturunku is a prominent Inca/Andean symbolic animal (also in 'uturunku achachi' legends), but the plain noun is everyday vocabulary. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

Common word for hummingbird; AMLQ spells it 'q'enti' (with e allophone written). Pronounced with e near q. Name also appears in place names (Q'intiq…). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

Kept existing draft. Native Quechua word (source of the Spanish). Alternatives: 'qarwa' (llama, esp. pale/yellowish in some sources), 'llamas' plural is -kuna: 'llamakuna'. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

Source of Spanish 'cóndor'. The condor is symbolically important (national emblem, ritual dances), but kuntur is the plain animal noun. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

Standard Cusco word for butterfly; variant 'pilpintu'. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976); Hornberger & Hornberger, Diccionario tri-lingüe Quechua of Cusco (1983).

review_question: What do you call a turkey (the farmyard bird, Spanish 'pavo') when speaking Quechua — 'pawu', 'pavo', or another word?
note: Turkey is a Mesoamerican domesticate with no native Andean name I can confirm. 'pawu' is a Spanish loan ('pavo') adapted to Quechua phonology; speakers may simply say 'pavo'. Do not confuse with native Andean birds (e.g. 'pawa' / guan, uncertain). Needs native-speaker check of what is actually said.

review_question: Is there a Quechua word you use for a turtle or tortoise, or do you say 'tortuga'? If the loan, how would you spell it?
note: Reviewer accepted: changed from 'charapa', which is a Peruvian-Amazon regional (probably not Quechua) word for the river turtle Podocnemis that I cannot defend as highland Cusco Quechua. Adapted Spanish loan per loan policy; speakers may say 'tortuga' unadapted.

Standard Cusco word for frog. Contrast 'hamp'atu' = toad; picture should be a frog. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: Do you pronounce the word for snake with a popped (ejective) ch' — 'mach'aqway' — or plain 'machaqway'?
note: Ordinary word for snake (variant spelling mach'aqway / machaqway). Deliberately NOT 'amaru', which is the mythic/great serpent with strong religious and political associations. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). Reviewer flag accepted: the ejective is uncertain — sources vary between 'mach'aqway' and 'machaqway'. Shares 'mach'a-' with mach'ay (cueva), so avoidWith.

Kept existing draft. Standard word for maize (plant and grain); 'choclo' (fresh ear) is 'chuqllu'. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

gloss: prickly-pear fruit (Opuntia); the plant is uncertain
review_question: The card shows a prickly-pear cactus plant with flat pads. Does 'tuna' name the plant or only the fruit? Is there another word for the plant (e.g. 'waraqu' or similar)?
note: Nopal is a Mexican term not used in Peru. In the Andes the Opuntia plant and fruit are called 'tuna', a word that entered via Spanish (originally Taíno), so it is labelled loanword. I do not know a confirmed native Quechua term; reviewers should check. Note the card art (nopal pads) may read as 'tuna' to Andean children. Reviewer point accepted: 'tuna' primarily names the fruit, not the pad/plant shown on the card.

Native word for bean, source of Southern Cone Spanish 'poroto'. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: For pineapple, do Quechua speakers say 'piña', or is 'achupalla' or another word used?
note: Pineapple is a lowland fruit; speakers generally use Spanish 'piña'. Colonial sources record 'achupalla' for pineapple/bromeliads, but today achupalla refers mainly to wild Puya bromeliads, so it would confuse. Labelled loanword.

Native generic word for Capsicum pepper (also 'hot spice'); the large rocoto is 'ruqut'u'. Domestic Andean Capsicum predates contact, so this is a genuine native word, not a Mesoamerican borrowing. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). Spelling of rocoto varies: 'ruqutu' vs 'ruqut'u'.

Kept existing draft. Native Quechua word (source of Spanish 'papa'). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: Is 'palta' felt as a Quechua word or as Spanish? Is there any other word for avocado?
note: Andean word for avocado, source of Peruvian Spanish 'palta' (traditionally linked to the Palta people of southern Ecuador). Used by Quechua speakers but may be perceived as Spanish; origin debated. Do not confuse with 'p'alta' (flat), ejective. Mesoamerican origin of the fruit: Nahuatl 'ahuacatl' is unrelated.

review_question: For tomato, do speakers say 'tumati', 'tomate', or another word? Which spelling would you use?
note: Reviewer accepted: adapted loan 'tumati' (trivocalic). Tomato word is Nahuatl via Spanish; no native Quechua term known to me.

review_question: For sunflower, do speakers say 'hirasul', 'girasol', or a Quechua phrase? Which spelling would you use?
note: Reviewer accepted: adapted loan, no /x/ or o (g→h, o→u), penultimate stress. Sunflower is a North American crop. A coined native phrase like 'inti qhawaq' (inti 'sun' + qhawa- 'look' + -q agentive) is NOT used: invented, and sun-cult flavoured.

Kept existing draft. Everyday word for the sun; also the name of the Inca sun deity (Inti). Card shows the celestial body, which is the ordinary sense. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

Kept existing draft. Moon; also means 'month'. Mama Killa is the moon deity, but 'killa' alone is the everyday noun. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

Standard word for star (AMLQ 'qoyllur'); o allophone before/after q. Also in the pilgrimage name Qoyllur Rit'i; the noun itself is ordinary. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
Rain (noun; verb 'para-' to rain). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: For a lightning bolt, would a child say 'illapa' or 'qhaqya'/'q'aqya'? Is 'illapa' too tied to the old deity or to 'gun' for a children's game?
note: Common word for lightning/thunderbolt; also the name of the Inca thunder/weather deity (Illapa) and colloquially 'gun'. Kept because it is the ordinary noun (like inti, killa), but flagged for reviewers. Alternative: 'q'aqya' (thunder / thunderbolt). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). Reviewer spells the alternative 'qhaqya' (aspirate); I had 'q'aqya' (ejective) — needs checking.

Standard word for rainbow. Folk belief: rainbows can cause illness (pregnant women and children are told not to point at it); reviewers may want to note this for children's use. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
Standard word for cloud (also mist). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

Standard word for wind. Note 'wayra' also figures in folk illness concepts ('mal viento'), but the noun is everyday. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: Is there a Quechua word for a comet? Would 'chupayuq quyllur' ('star with a tail') be understood, or would speakers just say 'cometa'?
note: Descriptive phrase: chupa 'tail' + -yuq 'possessor' + quyllur 'star'. I could not confirm a traditional single word for comet; colonial lexicons may record one, which reviewers should prefer if found. Could also simply be Spanish 'cometa'.

Plain word for mountain/hill (AMLQ 'orqo'). Deliberately NOT 'apu', which denotes a sacred mountain lord/spirit and is a ritual term. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). Note: 'urqu' also means 'male' (of animals, e.g. urqu llama), so it can be heard that way out of context.

review_question: Is 'nina urqu' ('fire mountain') understood as volcano, or do speakers say 'volcán'/'wulkan'? Does 'urqu' risk being heard as 'male' here?
note: Descriptive compound: nina 'fire' + urqu 'mountain'. No well-attested Cusco word for volcano known to me (Cusco has no active volcanoes); speakers likely say Spanish 'volcán'. Specific volcanoes (Misti, Sabancaya) are apu-type sacred peaks, so avoid naming one. Reviewers may prefer the loan. Shares 'urqu' with montana (avoidWith); 'urqu' also means 'male'.

Standard word for spring/well (Spanish 'puquio' derives from it). Springs are often places of offerings and are believed to have spirits; the noun itself is ordinary. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: Do you say 'lamar qucha' for the sea? Is 'mama qucha' better or too religious for a children's game?
note: Commonly used Cusco term for the sea: a hybrid of Spanish 'la mar' and Quechua qucha 'lake, body of water'. Alternative 'mama qucha' ('mother lake') is the colonial term but also names the sea deity Mamaqucha, so avoided as card word. Plain 'qucha' = lake, too broad. Source: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005) (lists lamar qocha).

review_question: How would you name a sandy desert: 'ch'aki pampa', 'purun', 'purun pampa', or the Spanish word?
note: Descriptive: ch'aki 'dry' + pampa 'plain, open flat land'. Alternative attested 'purun' / 'purun pampa' (wild, uninhabited, uncultivated land) — closer to colonial 'despoblado' than to a sandy desert. No desert in Cusco; reviewers decide.

review_question: For the tropical rainforest (many trees, rain, monkeys), would you say 'sach'a sach'a', 'yunka', 'anti', or another word?
note: Reviewer accepted: reduplicated sach'a 'tree, bush' + sach'a ('many trees' → thicket, forest); treated as descriptive, not a dictionary word for rainforest. Alternatives: 'yunka' (warm lowland zone), 'anti' (eastern lowlands; historical, as in Antisuyu).

review_question: Does 'qispi' mean a rock crystal to you? Could children confuse it with 'qispi' meaning 'free/saved'?
note: Qispi means crystal/glass/transparent stone (AMLQ 'qespi'); homophonous with qispi 'free, saved' (qispi- 'to escape, be saved'), which can be ambiguous. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: Is 'wat'a' the word you use for an island, or is it only known around Lake Titicaca?
note: Word for island used especially around Lake Titicaca (Puno/Collao); AMLQ lists wat'a 'isla'. Less familiar to speakers far from lakes. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005).

review_question: Do you pronounce the word for cave with an ejective, 'mach'ay'?
note: Standard word for cave/rock shelter (also 'machay' in place names). Caves can be associated with ancestors/spirits (and chinkana tunnels), but mach'ay is the ordinary noun. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
Standard word for (clay) cooking pot. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: What do you call a woven basket for carrying fruit: 'isanka', 'chiwi', or another word?
note: Word for a woven basket (cane/reed) in Cusco dictionaries. Regional alternatives exist (e.g. 'chiwi', 'wayunka' uncertain); reviewers should pick the local everyday word. Sources: Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976); Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005).

review_question: For a drum played with hands or sticks, which word do children know: 'wankar', 'tinya', or another?
note: Wankar / wankara = drum (Spanish 'huancar'); attested in colonial and modern dictionaries. Today 'tinya' names the small hand drum, 'wankar' a larger drum; either may be expected. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976). 'tinya' may be the better everyday word for a small hand drum.

Tika = sun-dried adobe brick (verb 'tikay' to make adobes). Not to be confused with t'ika 'flower' (ejective) — reviewers must check pronunciation/orthography carefully. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).
Standard word for spun thread/yarn. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: For a small boat paddled on a lake, would you say 'wampu', 'balsa', 'tuytu', or another word?
note: Wampu = boat/raft in colonial and modern dictionaries; canoe-specific terms are Amazonian. On Lake Titicaca reed boats are 'balsa' (Spanish) or 'tuytu'(uncertain). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

Standard word for bridge (as in Q'iswachaka, the woven grass bridge). Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: For a wax candle, do you say 'wila', 'vela', or something else? Which spelling would you use?
note: Spanish 'vela' adapted to Quechua phonology; candles are post-contact. Speakers may also just say 'vela'. Note 'wila' resembles Aymara 'wila' (red/blood). Candles are central in offerings; fine as a household object.

review_question: For a hammer, do you say 'martillu' or 'martillo', and is there any native word?
note: Spanish loan; the metal claw hammer is post-contact. I do not know a reliable native term for hammer (hammerstones existed, but I cannot confirm the word), so no native form is proposed.
Standard word for house/home. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: Is 'chakra' a good name for a field where maize, beans and squash grow together, or would you add something (e.g. 'sara chakra')?
note: Reviewer suggestion partly accepted: changed from 'sara chakra' to plain 'chakra' so it does not repeat 'sara' (maiz card). Kind kept as attested, not descriptive: chakra is a single dictionary word (source of Spanish 'chacra'), used here as an approximate equivalent — Andean chakra is any field, not specifically Mesoamerican maize–bean–squash intercropping.

review_question: For a small neighbourhood shop, would you say 'tinda', 'tienda', or 'qhatu'? Is 'qhatu' only a market?
note: Reviewer accepted: changed from 'qhatu', which means market/market stall (Spanish 'cato'), not a neighbourhood shop. Adapted loan per loan policy (ie→i). 'qhatu' remains an option if reviewers prefer a native word with a broader meaning.

review_question: For the town square, do you say 'plasa', 'plaza', or 'pampa'? Would you spell it with an initial cluster ('plasa') or another way?
note: Spanish loan in common use. Native 'pampa' (open flat ground) was used for Inca plazas (Hawk'aypata, Kusipata), but pampa alone means 'plain', so the loan is clearer.

review_question: For a harbour where boats tie up, would you say 'pwirtu', 'puerto', or another word? Would 'puerto' make you think of a mountain pass instead?
note: Reviewer accepted: spelling decision 'pwirtu' (ue→wi, o→u). Risk: in Andean Spanish 'puerto' also means a mountain pass, so the loan may be heard as 'pass'. Cusco is inland; no traditional word known. Invented 'wampu samana' not used.

Standard word for town/village/settlement (AMLQ 'llaqta'). Also means 'country/people'. Smaller hamlet: 'ayllu' (kin community, socially loaded) — avoided. Sources: Academia Mayor de la Lengua Quechua, Diccionario Quechua–Español–Quechua (2005); Cusihuamán, Diccionario Quechua Cuzco–Collao (1976).

review_question: For school, do children say 'yachay wasi' or 'iskuyla'?
note: Descriptive compound: yacha- 'know, learn' + -y nominalizer + wasi 'house'. Widely used in Peruvian bilingual education (Ministerio de Educación EIB materials) and historically for the Inca 'yachaywasi'. Everyday speech often uses Spanish loan 'iskuyla'.

review_question: Would 'quyllur qhawana wasi' ('house for watching stars') be understood as an observatory, or would speakers say 'observatorio'?
note: Descriptive: quyllur 'star' + qhawa- 'look, watch' + -na 'instrument/place' + wasi 'house'. Invented for this card, not attested; no institutional neologism known to me. Speakers would likely say 'observatorio'.

review_question: For a library, is there an established Quechua term (e.g. from schools or the Academia)? If 'liwru wasi', do you spell it 'liwru' or 'libru'?
note: Descriptive with a Spanish loan root: liwru (< 'libro') + wasi 'house'. Some EIB/AMLQ neologism lists use other forms (e.g. 'maytu wasi' or 'qillqa wasi'), which I cannot verify; reviewers should replace with any established institutional term. Loan root spelling uncertain: 'liwru' vs 'libru'.
